If the person is fully alert and able to swallow, I would give cyproheptadine early, since it blocks serotonin receptors. So far, the evidence for this med has only been case reports, and a recent review found them insufficient to show that it works. I wouldn't wait to see whether it does before doing the other steps. And most people won't have it at home anyway, since it needs a prescription in the US, though a telehealth doctor might write one quickly, and only some countries sell it without one.

While you wait, you might think of this guide's other remedies, like niacin for ending a trip or DMSO for brain injuries, seizures and chest pain, but I wouldn't use either one here. Niacin is actually unsafe with serotonin syndrome, since at the doses used to end a trip it can cause flushing, dizziness and low blood pressure (NIH). I'd also leave out this guide's Syrian rue oil for now: made at home it has almost none of the harmala alkaloids, but I couldn't find any research on it with MDMA, so it could help or harm here. Magnesium chloride is the one I would consider, since many people with serotonin syndrome run low on magnesium (a nursing review). If they're fully alert and able to swallow, I'd give it by mouth, especially with MDMA-related jaw tension or muscle activity (the amounts are in MDMA: Magnesium Alarm, above). Topical magnesium chloride if they're not able to swallow.

The ER doctors will want to know exactly what they took, so before the ambulance comes, I'd gather their pill bottles and packages. I'd also jot down how much of each they took and when, street drugs and supplements included. Keep track of how their breathing is doing, as that's one of the main indicators of how dangerous the seizure is, according to the CDC.
